title: Permission: getting the go-ahead
subtitle: accede to, condone, veto, carte blanche
summary: Use the formal, newspaper vocabulary of permission and prohibition - accede, acquiesce, endorse, veto, outlaw, clamp down - with the prepositions they demand.

lesson.heading: Verbs for permitting and agreeing
rows: accede (to)
accept, but often after initial unwillingness
The factory owner acceded to the workers' demands.
acquiesce (in/to)
permit something to happen, often with a degree of secrecy or conspiracy
The Foreign Minister acquiesced in the plan to restrict imports from certain countries.
assent (to)
agree to something, often plans, proposals or ideas
The shareholders assented to the takeover.
authorise
give official permission
Only authorised people are allowed entry.
condone
approve or allow something most people consider wrong
The judge condoned the use of reasonable force by police officers.
countenance
consider giving assent or permission; often used in negative contexts
No government would ever countenance abolishing taxes altogether.
endorse
give official approval to something
The cabinet has endorsed a proposal to change the way universities are funded.
lesson.note: All of these verbs are formal, and many of them are typical newspaper words.

lesson.heading: Shades of agreement
lesson.text: The difference is in the attitude behind the agreement. To **accede** is to give in at last; to **acquiesce** is to let something happen quietly, often without admitting it openly; to **condone** or **countenance** is to accept something other people think is wrong; to **endorse** is to approve publicly and officially.

examples.text: The President finally had to **accede to** demands for his resignation.
The newspaper revealed that the Prime Minister had **acquiesced in** the secret decision to sell arms to the dictator.
I would never **condone** the use of capital punishment, no matter how serious the crime.
The manager has **authorised** the wearing of casual clothes to work on Friday.

lesson.heading: Phrasal expressions for permission
lesson.text: To be given **carte blanche** is to have complete freedom to do whatever you think necessary - a formal expression borrowed from French. To be given **the go-ahead for** something, or **the green light to** something, is the informal equivalent: permission for work to start.

examples.text: The committee have been given **carte blanche** to investigate the problem and come up with a solution.
The city has given **the go-ahead for** the new car park.
The college principal has given **the green light to** the students' proposal for an end-of-term festival.

lesson.heading: Verbs for prohibiting and disapproving
rows: bar (from)
officially exclude someone, forbid them access to something
Three students were barred from using the library because they had damaged books.
clamp down (on)
use your full power to prevent or limit something
The government has decided to clamp down on illegal immigration.
outlaw
make something illegal
Parliament has passed a bill outlawing smoking while driving.
veto
use your official power to forbid
The President has vetoed the plan to open membership of the club to the public.

lesson.heading: The prepositions to memorise
rows: accede to
He would never accede to the union's demands.
acquiesce in / to
The Minister is likely to acquiesce in the proposal.
assent to
The President has assented to the latest world environment plan.
clamp down on
It's time the police clamped down on cyclists going through red lights.
bar someone from
She has been barred from lectures.
the green light to / the go-ahead for
given the green light to the proposal; given the go-ahead for a new factory
carte blanche to do something
The inspector had carte blanche to investigate every aspect of the business.

lesson.heading: More permission words from the news
lesson.text: An **embargo** is an official prohibition on something; if it is cancelled, it is **lifted**. A **franchise** is permission to operate a service or commercial activity, usually for a set period. **Zero tolerance** means that not even the smallest crime or misbehaviour will be allowed, and **sanctions** are restrictions imposed on some activity.

examples.text: Government to **lift** the **embargo** on computer imports - at present, chips and processors must be home-produced.
Railway **franchise** extended for five years: the company will be allowed to run services for the additional period.
Police to adopt **zero tolerance** of hooliganism: anyone displaying threatening behaviour will be liable to immediate arrest.
New trade **sanctions** announced: firms hope to benefit from less severe competition in domestic markets.

lesson.text: **Regardless** is an adverb, not an adjective. Use it alone - she went **regardless** - or with **of**: **regardless of** the fact that they had no planning permission. Never ~~regardless to~~.

exercises.prompt: The committee were in favour of the proposal, but the President ___ it.
exercises.hint: (past tense; used official power to forbid it)
exercises.explanation: To veto something is to use your official power to forbid it.

exercises.prompt: I would never ___ the use of capital punishment, no matter how serious the crime.
exercises.explanation: Condone and countenance both mean to approve or allow something that most people consider wrong.

exercises.prompt: The newspaper revealed that the Prime Minister had ___ in the secret decision to sell arms to the dictator.
exercises.hint: (past participle; agreed without openly admitting it)
exercises.explanation: To acquiesce in something is to permit it to happen, often with a degree of secrecy.

exercises.prompt: The new bill going through Parliament will ___ the use of unlicensed drugs by doctors.
exercises.explanation: To outlaw something is to make it illegal.

exercises.prompt: The President finally had to ___ to demands for his resignation.
exercises.explanation: To accede to something is to accept it, often after initial unwillingness.

exercises.prompt: She has been ___ from lectures because she disrupted one last term.
exercises.explanation: To bar someone from something is to officially exclude them from it.

exercises.prompt: Alex parked his car outside the shop regardless ___ the No Parking sign.
exercises.explanation: Regardless is an adverb; it is followed by of when a phrase comes next.

exercises.prompt: It's time the police clamped down ___ cyclists going through red lights.
exercises.explanation: Clamp down on something means use your full power to prevent or limit it.

exercises.prompt: The President has assented ___ the latest world environment plan.
exercises.explanation: Assent to something - agree to a plan, proposal or idea.

exercises.prompt: The company has been given the go-ahead ___ a new factory in the city.
exercises.explanation: Give the go-ahead for something, but give the green light to something.

exercises.prompt: The manager has ___ the wearing of casual clothes to work on Friday.
exercises.explanation: To authorise is to give official permission; endorse would also be possible.

exercises.prompt: The police have announced that they are to begin to ___ on motorists who exceed the speed limit.
exercises.explanation: To clamp down on something is to take serious action to reduce it.

exercises.prompt: The inspector had carte blanche ___ every aspect of the business.
exercises.explanation: Carte blanche is followed by to + verb; it means complete freedom to do whatever you think necessary.

exercises.statement: If an embargo is lifted, the prohibition is cancelled.
exercises.explanation: Correct - an embargo is an official prohibition, and to lift it is to remove it.

exercises.statement: 'She went to the party regardless the warning' is correct English.
exercises.explanation: No - regardless is an adverb: she went regardless, or regardless of the warning.

exercises.answer: The committee have been given carte blanche to investigate the problem
exercises.explanation: Carte blanche is complete freedom to do whatever you think necessary.
